stem:
A 4-month-old girl born at 38 weeks presents to your regional emergency department in July with 3 days of coryza and worsening cough. She is feeding at half her usual volume, has had four wet nappies in 24 hours, and had a brief apnoeic pause at home that resolved with stimulation.

On examination she is alert, mildly tachypnoeic with subcostal recession, and has bilateral fine crackles and wheeze. There is no fever. She has no prior admissions and was well until this illness.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 152, BP 88/54, RR 62, SpO2 89% on room air, temp 37.2 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; capillary refill 2 seconds; peripheries warm; subcostal and intercostal recession; nasal flare absent; bilateral fine crackles with expiratory wheeze
data_table.Investigations: Bedside blood glucose 4.6 mmol/L; NPA pending; chest x-ray not yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial oxygen therapy?

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg with 6 litres per minute driving oxygen with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Bronchodilators are not recommended in bronchiolitis in this age group and driving oxygen through a nebuliser is not the correct route. Salbutamol has not been shown to alter the natural history of bronchiolitis and RCH recommends against routine use. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: High-flow nasal cannula oxygen at 2 litres per kilogram per minute from the outset with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: HFNC is not first-line in RCH-aligned practice; it is escalation therapy for infants who fail low-flow after 2 hours. Starting HFNC immediately in a child who has not yet had a low-flow trial is over-escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Face mask oxygen at 6 litres per minute, titrate to SpO2 at least 94 percent with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: The RCH SpO2 target in bronchiolitis is 90 percent, not 94 percent, because higher targets prolong length of stay without benefit. Face mask delivery is also poorly tolerated by infants and is not the standard first-line device. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Continuous positive airway pressure via mask at 5 cm H2O with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: CPAP is a paediatric intensive care escalation used for impending respiratory failure not responsive to HFNC. It is not indicated as the initial oxygen device on the general ward. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Nasal prong oxygen at 1 litre per minute, titrate to SpO2 at least 90 percent with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: RCH CPG for bronchiolitis specifies low-flow nasal prong oxygen (1-2 L/min) as first-line for hypoxia, with a target SpO2 of 90 percent. HFNC is reserved for failure of low-flow after 2 hours of observation. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: This infant has moderate bronchiolitis with hypoxia (SpO2 89 percent) and increased work of breathing but is alert with adequate perfusion. RCH CPG mandates low-flow nasal prong oxygen (1-2 L/min) titrated to an SpO2 target of 90 percent as first-line. HFNC is escalation therapy after a documented low-flow failure. This shifts practice away from earlier North American 92-94 percent targets and pre-emptive HFNC.
key_points: Low-flow nasal prong 1-2 L/min is first-line oxygen delivery for bronchiolitis at RCH
SpO2 target is at least 90 percent, not 92-94 percent
HFNC is reserved for failure of low-flow after 2 hours
Salbutamol is not routinely recommended in bronchiolitis under 12 months
explanation.pearls: Escalating to HFNC before trialling low-flow for 2 hours over-medicalises stable bronchiolitis; document the low-flow trial before you step up.

stem:
A 2-year-old boy is brought in at 2 am with barking cough and hoarse voice starting after a coryzal illness. His mother says he sounds noisy on breathing in when upset but is quiet when settled on her lap.

On examination he is settled, has a barking cough, and stridor is audible only with agitation. There is mild suprasternal recession when he cries but none at rest. Air entry is symmetrical and there is no wheeze.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 96/58, RR 32, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temp 37.6 C
data_table.Examination: Alert, comforted by mother; barking cough; stridor with agitation only; mild suprasternal recession when crying, none at rest

lead_in: What dose of dexamethasone would you give?

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg per kg once now with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: This child has mild croup (Westley 1-2) - stridor with agitation only, no rest stridor, minimal recession. RCH CPG specifies oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg per kg for mild and moderate croup; the higher 0.6 mg per kg dose is reserved for severe croup with rest stridor and marked recession. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg per kg once now with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: 0.6 mg per kg is the severe croup dose. Using it for mild croup delivers four times the required steroid load without added benefit in mild disease, and this child has no rest stridor. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Nebulised budesonide 2 mg once now instead of dexamethasone
options.rationale: Nebulised budesonide is second-line and used when oral is not tolerated (persistent vomiting, unable to swallow). Oral dexamethasone is preferred first-line at RCH because it is cheaper, longer-acting, and does not require agitation with a mask. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg per kg once now with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Prednisolone has shorter duration than dexamethasone and higher relapse rates in croup; RCH prefers dexamethasone. Prednisolone is a legitimate alternative only when dexamethasone is unavailable. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Withhold steroid and reassess after 30 minutes of observation
options.rationale: Mild croup still benefits from a single dose of dexamethasone (reduced re-presentation and symptom duration); RCH recommends steroid for all severity tiers of croup. Withholding delays benefit and misses discharge on the same visit. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Mild croup at RCH is treated with oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg per kg as a single dose, not the severe-croup 0.6 mg per kg dose. The severity tier is decided by rest stridor and work of breathing at rest, not stridor with agitation. All severity tiers get a steroid dose because it reduces relapse and re-presentation.
key_points: Mild and moderate croup: dexamethasone 0.15 mg per kg orally single dose
Severe croup with rest stridor: 0.6 mg per kg orally, plus nebulised adrenaline
Nebulised budesonide is reserved for children unable to tolerate oral
Prednisolone has higher relapse and is not first-line at RCH
explanation.pearls: Stridor with agitation but not at rest is mild croup - 0.15 mg per kg dexamethasone once is enough.

stem:
A 3-year-old girl weighing 15 kg develops a widespread urticarial rash, hoarse voice, and repeated coughing within 5 minutes of eating a peanut biscuit at daycare. Paramedics report she vomited twice on the way to your ED.

On arrival she looks anxious, has audible stridor at rest, and has swollen lips. Circulation is preserved and she is protecting her airway. There is no wheeze on auscultation but transmitted upper airway noise is loud. She has a known peanut allergy on the daycare register.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148, BP 92/56, RR 34, SpO2 95 percent on room air, temp 36.9 C
data_table.Examination: Widespread urticaria trunk and face; peri-oral and lip swelling; audible stridor at rest; no wheeze; capillary refill 2 seconds

lead_in: What dose of intramuscular adrenaline would you administer first?

options.text: Adrenaline 300 micrograms intramuscularly to the anterolateral thigh
options.rationale: 300 mcg is the ASCIA banded dose for children over 20 kg (EpiPen adult). At 15 kg this doubles the correct dose and increases risk of tachyarrhythmia. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines 2023)

options.text: Adrenaline 150 micrograms intramuscularly to the anterolateral thigh
options.rationale: ASCIA banded dosing for children 10-20 kg is adrenaline 150 mcg IM (0.15 mL of 1:1000). This child is 15 kg and sits squarely in the 10-20 kg band. Using the banded table rather than mg per kg arithmetic reduces dose error under time pressure. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines 2023)

options.text: Adrenaline 10 micrograms per kg intramuscularly, calculated to 150 micrograms
options.rationale: The ASCIA standard is a banded weight table, not per-kg calculation, precisely to avoid arithmetic errors during a resuscitation. Although 10 mcg per kg happens to give the same answer at 15 kg, teaching or documenting per-kg arithmetic in adrenaline for anaphylaxis is discouraged in AU practice. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines 2023)

options.text: Adrenaline 150 micrograms subcutaneously to the anterolateral thigh
options.rationale: Subcutaneous absorption is slower and less predictable than intramuscular in shock; ASCIA and ANZCOR require IM into the anterolateral thigh. Wrong route is a common exam trap. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines 2023)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 while preparing IM dose
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline may be added as adjunct for upper airway oedema after IM adrenaline is given, but never as a substitute for the first IM dose. Nebulised alone does not treat systemic anaphylaxis. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines 2023)

explanation.summary: Rest stridor with a widespread urticarial rash after peanut exposure is anaphylaxis by ASCIA criteria. First-line is IM adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh at the banded weight dose - 150 mcg for 10-20 kg and 300 mcg for over 20 kg. Australian practice deliberately avoids mg per kg arithmetic for adrenaline in anaphylaxis to reduce dosing errors.
key_points: Anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline to anterolateral thigh, first-line
ASCIA banded dose: 150 mcg for 10-20 kg (EpiPen Jr); 300 mcg for over 20 kg (EpiPen)
Do not calculate mg per kg during the resuscitation
Nebulised adrenaline is adjunct, never a substitute
explanation.pearls: Banded weight tables save lives when the calculator is slow - 15 kg gets 150 mcg without arithmetic.

stem:
A 21-day-old boy born at term by uncomplicated vaginal birth is brought to your ED at 3 am. Parents report he has been feeding poorly for 8 hours and had one axillary temperature of 38.3 C at home. He is now afebrile but they describe him as floppy.

On examination he is pale, minimally responsive to nappy change, and has cool peripheries with a capillary refill of 3.5 seconds. Anterior fontanelle is normal. Skin examination shows no rash. Chest is clear and abdomen is soft. There is no organomegaly.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 190, BP 62 systolic, RR 68, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temp 36.1 C
data_table.Examination: Pale, hypotonic, minimally responsive; capillary refill 3.5 s; anterior fontanelle normal; no rash; chest clear; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 2.4 mmol/L; VBG pH 7.22, lactate 4.8 mmol/L, base excess -9

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management priority?

options.text: Intranasal midazolam for agitation, then oral maintenance rehydration once settled with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: This infant is not agitated; he is hypotonic and shocked. Sedation would worsen respiratory drive and cardiovascular status. Oral rehydration cannot address septic shock. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

options.text: IV access, blood cultures, empirical IV ceftriaxone with cardiac monitoring with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is contraindicated in neonates because of bilirubin displacement and calcium precipitation risk; cefotaxime is the third-generation cephalosporin of choice under 28 days. This choice also omits benzylpenicillin for Listeria and does not correct the documented hypoglycaemia. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

options.text: Peripheral IV, blood cultures, and empirical IV amoxicillin with cardiac monitoring with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Amoxicillin plus gentamicin is a legitimate early neonatal regimen but at 21 days the RCH pathway shifts to cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin because meningitis pathogen spectrum broadens. LP should not delay first-dose antibiotics or fluid resuscitation in a shocked infant; do LP after stabilisation. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

options.text: IV access, blood cultures, empirical IV cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: This is a shocked hypoglycaemic neonate. RCH neonatal sepsis pathway for infants under 28 days requires IV access, blood cultures, and empirical broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within the hour (cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin for Listeria cover), correction of hypoglycaemia with 2 mL per kg of 10 percent dextrose, and fluid resuscitation with 20 mL per kg boluses. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

options.text: Warm and observe with hourly vital signs; hold antibiotics until cultures return with cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Withholding antibiotics in a shocked neonate would result in preventable death; first-dose antibiotics are targeted within the hour. Cultures inform, not gate, antibiotic timing. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

explanation.summary: A neonate presenting hypotonic, poorly perfused, hypoglycaemic and acidotic after a fever at home has septic shock until proven otherwise. RCH pathway for infants under 28 days combines cefotaxime (not ceftriaxone) plus benzylpenicillin for Listeria cover, IV dextrose 10 percent 2 mL per kg for hypoglycaemia, and 20 mL per kg normal saline boluses. LP is performed once stabilised so as not to delay first-dose antibiotics.
key_points: Neonates under 28 days: cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin (not ceftriaxone)
Correct hypoglycaemia with 10 percent dextrose 2 mL per kg
Fluid boluses 20 mL per kg over 5 to 10 minutes, repeat to 60 mL per kg then inotropes
LP after stabilisation - never before first-dose antibiotics in a shocked infant
explanation.pearls: Ceftriaxone is a paediatric go-to but is contraindicated in the neonate for bilirubin and calcium reasons - swap to cefotaxime under 28 days.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management
eTG complete: Neonatal sepsis empirical therapy

stem:
A 3-year-old girl is referred by her GP after 11 days of fever. Over that time she has developed a rash, red cracked lips, a red tongue, and bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis. Peeling has started around her fingertips this morning. The parents say the fever came down for the first time yesterday.

On examination she has mild peri-anal desquamation and desquamating fingertips, a single 2 cm cervical lymph node, and a diffuse maculopapular rash on her trunk. Cardiac auscultation is unremarkable and there is no gallop.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 96/60, RR 26, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temp 37.4 C
data_table.Investigations: Hb 96 g/L (110-140); WCC 16.4 x10^9/L (4-11); platelets 620 x10^9/L (150-450); CRP 78 mg/L (<5); ALT 74 U/L (<40); albumin 28 g/L (35-50); sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145); urine white cells positive with negative culture
data_table.Echocardiogram: Left main coronary artery Z-score +2.2, right coronary artery Z-score +1.6, no aneurysm; normal LV function

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.text: IV methylprednisolone pulse for 3 days and no immunoglobulin with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Corticosteroid monotherapy is not first-line; adjunctive steroid is considered in IVIG-resistant disease or high-risk primary treatment, but always in combination with IVIG, not as a substitute. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Oral aspirin at antiplatelet dose alone and outpatient echocardiogram follow up in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Antiplatelet aspirin alone under-treats active disease; without IVIG the coronary risk continues to accrue while systemic inflammation persists (CRP still 78, platelets 620). Follow-up echo is appropriate but is not the current management priority. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: IV immunoglobulin 2 g per kg over 10 to 12 hours plus oral aspirin at anti-inflammatory dose
options.rationale: This is late-presenting Kawasaki disease meeting classical criteria with laboratory support and borderline coronary Z-scores. Even after day 10, if there is ongoing inflammation (raised CRP or platelets) or coronary abnormality, IVIG plus aspirin is still indicated. Australian and international consensus supports IVIG in late presenters with these findings. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Oral ibuprofen for symptom control and reassure that peeling means the illness has run its course
options.rationale: The disease is not over just because desquamation has begun; coronary complications develop after the acute phase in untreated Kawasaki. NSAIDs do not modify coronary risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Discharge home on watchful waiting because the fever has settled without treatment
options.rationale: Fever resolution without treatment is not reassurance in Kawasaki disease. Coronary aneurysms develop over subsequent weeks; discharging without IVIG in a case with ongoing inflammation is a serious under-treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

explanation.summary: This girl meets classical Kawasaki criteria (fever plus 4 of 5 principal features), has supportive labs (raised CRP, thrombocytosis, hypoalbuminaemia, sterile pyuria, hyponatraemia, anaemia, transaminitis) and borderline coronary dilatation. Even beyond day 10, if inflammation or coronary changes persist, IVIG 2 g per kg plus aspirin remains indicated because coronary morbidity continues to accrue.
key_points: Late-presenting Kawasaki still warrants IVIG if ongoing inflammation or coronary changes
IVIG dose is 2 g per kg over 10 to 12 hours as a single infusion
Aspirin is added at anti-inflammatory dose in the acute phase, then reduced to antiplatelet
Steroid is adjunctive for high-risk or IVIG-refractory disease, not a substitute
explanation.pearls: Kawasaki does not have a day-10 IVIG cut-off - if CRP is still up or the coronaries are dilating, give IVIG.

stem:
A 4-year-old girl presents to your rural ED collapsed on the trolley with a history of 24 hours of vomiting and reduced urine output. On arrival she has a purpuric rash on her thighs and cool mottled peripheries.

The nurse has attempted two peripheral IV cannulations in the antecubital fossae unsuccessfully over 4 minutes. She remains poorly perfused with a capillary refill of 5 seconds and is drowsy but rousable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, BP 68 systolic, RR 38, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temp 39.4 C
data_table.Examination: Non-blanching purpuric rash lower limbs and buttocks; capillary refill 5 s; peripheries cool and mottled; GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6)
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 5.8 mmol/L; POC lactate 5.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the next best step?

options.text: Central venous line insertion in the right internal jugular vein under ultrasound
options.rationale: CVL insertion is skill dependent and takes 15 to 20 minutes in a shocked small child in a rural ED; it is not the emergency access route. IO is faster and safer under these conditions. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 12.5)
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline 12.5 Paediatric advanced life support

options.text: Continue attempting peripheral IV access for a further 5 minutes before considering IO
options.rationale: ANZCOR sets a 90 second failure window for IV in a critical child before moving to IO, not a further 5 minutes. Prolonging IV attempts in a shocked child delays antibiotics and fluid resuscitation and increases mortality. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 12.5)
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline 12.5 Paediatric advanced life support

options.text: Insert an intraosseous needle in the proximal tibia and draw cultures with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: In a shocked child with meningococcal features and two failed IV attempts within a few minutes, IO access is the next step by ANZCOR paediatric ALS. Blood cultures may be drawn from the IO trocar; do not delay first-dose IV antibiotic and fluid resuscitation. Ceftriaxone at 50 mg per kg is empiric for suspected meningococcal disease over 28 days. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

options.text: IM ceftriaxone 50 mg per kg and continue attempting IV access with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: IM route in a shocked child has erratic absorption due to poor peripheral perfusion; the drug will not reach therapeutic levels in time. IO gives immediate central circulation delivery. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

options.text: Rectal paracetamol 15 mg per kg and re-attempt peripheral IV access when the fever settles
options.rationale: Antipyretic does not treat sepsis and fever reduction is not the driver of tachycardia in septic shock. Delaying antibiotics for symptomatic control worsens outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

explanation.summary: In a shocked child with a purpuric rash and two failed IV attempts, the next step is intraosseous access with blood cultures drawn from the trocar, followed by IV ceftriaxone and a 20 mL per kg saline bolus. ANZCOR paediatric ALS sets a 90 second window for IV before moving to IO in the critical child.
key_points: IO after 90 seconds of failed IV in a critical child
Blood cultures can be drawn from the IO trocar
Empiric IV ceftriaxone 50 mg per kg for suspected meningococcal disease over 28 days
First fluid bolus 20 mL per kg over 5 to 10 min, repeat to 60 mL per kg before inotropes
explanation.pearls: IO is the emergency access route in shocked children - 90 seconds of failed IV is enough, do not keep trying.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management
ANZCOR Guideline 12.5 Paediatric advanced life support

stem:
A 2-year-old boy with known congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency) on hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone is brought in with 18 hours of vomiting and lethargy. His parents doubled his oral hydrocortisone at illness onset but he has vomited every dose since. There has been no diarrhoea.

On examination he is drowsy but rousable, has cool peripheries with a capillary refill of 4 seconds, and mucous membranes are dry. Skin turgor is reduced. There is no focal infection on examination and the abdomen is soft with no organomegaly.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 172, BP 74/40, RR 32, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temp 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, capillary refill 4 s; dry mucous membranes; reduced skin turgor; abdomen soft; no rash
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 122 mmol/L (135-145); potassium 6.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); glucose 2.6 mmol/L (3.5-6.0); urea 12 mmol/L (2.5-7.5); VBG pH 7.24, HCO3 14 mmol/L, base excess -10; POC lactate 3.2 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: Hydrocortisone 5 mg orally three times daily; fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Double the oral hydrocortisone dose and admit for observation and repeat as clinically indicated
options.rationale: The child is already vomiting the oral hydrocortisone; that route has failed. Oral cannot be relied on in a crisis - parenteral hydrocortisone is required, and observation alone is inadequate treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal crisis)

options.text: IV dexamethasone 0.15 mg per kg then oral rehydration when tolerated and repeat as clinically indicated
options.rationale: Dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid activity and cannot correct hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia in an adrenal crisis; hydrocortisone is required for its mineralocorticoid effect at stress doses. Oral rehydration cannot correct dehydration and hypoglycaemia here. (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal crisis)

options.text: Calcium gluconate 0.5 mL per kg IV followed by insulin dextrose infusion for hyperkalaemia
options.rationale: Insulin dextrose is inappropriate first-line in adrenal crisis with hypoglycaemia and may cause severe rebound; the hyperkalaemia here is driven by mineralocorticoid deficiency and reverses with hydrocortisone and fluid. Calcium is only indicated for ECG changes attributable to hyperkalaemia. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: 3 percent saline 3 mL per kg over 20 minutes for the hyponatraemia and repeat as clinically indicated
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizure or coma) with truly hypotonic hyponatraemia. Adrenal crisis hyponatraemia corrects with hydrocortisone and normal saline; hypertonic saline risks osmotic demyelination and is not indicated here. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyponatraemia)

options.text: IV hydrocortisone 50 mg stat plus 10 percent dextrose 2 mL per kg IV then normal saline 20 mL per kg over 30 minutes
options.rationale: This is adrenal crisis with documented hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia. Immediate parenteral hydrocortisone stress dose (50 mg for 1-5 years, 100 mg for over 5 years, 25 mg for under 1 year) is life-saving; oral cannot be relied on because he is vomiting. Glucose correction with 10 percent dextrose 2 mL per kg and volume resuscitation with normal saline are simultaneous priorities. (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal crisis)

explanation.summary: A known CAH child with vomiting, drowsiness, hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia has adrenal crisis. Parenteral hydrocortisone stress dose is required immediately - dexamethasone will not do the job because it lacks the mineralocorticoid activity needed to correct the hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia. Simultaneous glucose correction and fluid resuscitation are life-saving.
key_points: Adrenal crisis stress dose IV hydrocortisone: 25 mg under 1 y, 50 mg 1-5 y, 100 mg over 5 y
Hydrocortisone has mineralocorticoid activity at stress doses; dexamethasone does not
Correct hypoglycaemia with 10 percent dextrose 2 mL per kg, resuscitate with normal saline 20 mL per kg
Hyperkalaemia in adrenal crisis usually corrects with hydrocortisone and fluid, not insulin dextrose
explanation.pearls: Dexamethasone is the classic wrong answer in adrenal crisis - it does not touch the mineralocorticoid deficit driving the electrolyte derangement.

stem:
An 8-year-old girl with known asthma on daily fluticasone presents with acute severe wheeze at rest and inability to complete sentences. She has received back-to-back nebulised salbutamol 5 mg every 20 minutes for one hour, ipratropium 250 mcg on the first neb, and oral prednisolone 2 mg per kg 30 minutes ago. Her mother has given her a puff of salbutamol every hour since school pickup 4 hours ago.

After one hour of nebulised therapy she is still speaking in single words with marked subcostal recession, silent chest is not present but air entry is reduced globally, and SpO2 is 90 percent on 10 L via non-rebreather mask. She has become tremulous.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, BP 108/68, RR 44, SpO2 90 percent on non-rebreather, temp 37.1 C
data_table.Examination: Speaking in single words; marked subcostal recession; global reduced air entry with widespread wheeze; tremor
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.32, pCO2 44 mmHg (32-42), HCO3 22 mmol/L, lactate 4.2 mmol/L; potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); glucose 8.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Aminophylline loading 10 mg per kg over 60 minutes then maintenance infusion
options.rationale: Aminophylline is a later step used only when both magnesium and IV salbutamol fail; narrow therapeutic index and risk of arrhythmia make it a last-resort agent in AU paediatric practice. Skipping magnesium to jump to aminophylline is not supported. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

options.text: IV salbutamol loading 15 mcg per kg over 10 minutes then infusion at 1 mcg per kg per minute
options.rationale: IV salbutamol is used when magnesium fails or is contraindicated; RCH sequences magnesium first because it has a better safety profile and comparable efficacy in children. Her potassium 3.1 mmol/L and lactate 4.2 mmol/L reflect ongoing beta-agonist toxicity from continuous salbutamol - adding IV salbutamol now would worsen both. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

options.text: IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg per kg (max 2 g) over 20 minutes with cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: This child has severe asthma failing maximal inhaled therapy. RCH CPG for severe asthma escalates with IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg per kg (max 2 g) over 20 minutes as the first IV bronchodilator, before IV salbutamol or aminophylline. Rising pCO2 into the normal range in a tachypnoeic asthmatic signals impending respiratory failure. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

options.text: Continue back-to-back nebulised salbutamol every 20 minutes and observe for 2 hours
options.rationale: One hour of maximal inhaled therapy has failed - continuing without escalation risks respiratory failure. Her lactate and hypokalaemia already reflect beta-agonist toxicity; more inhaled salbutamol worsens both without further bronchodilation. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

options.text: Ketamine 1 mg per kg intravenously for bronchodilation before RSI intubation
options.rationale: Ketamine at induction dose is used only when intubation for respiratory failure is decided; premature intubation of severe asthma before magnesium and IV salbutamol have been trialled worsens outcome because ventilation of stiff, hyperinflated lungs is very hazardous. Magnesium is the correct next step. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

explanation.summary: A child with severe asthma who has failed one hour of maximal inhaled bronchodilators and steroids, with rising pCO2 into the normal range, hypokalaemia, and lactic acidosis, needs IV escalation. RCH sequences IV magnesium sulfate first, IV salbutamol second, and aminophylline last. Repeating what has already failed or premature intubation both worsen outcome.
key_points: IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg per kg (max 2 g) is the first IV escalation in AU paediatric severe asthma
Rising pCO2 into normal range in tachypnoeic asthma signals fatigue and impending failure
Hypokalaemia and lactic acidosis reflect beta-agonist toxicity, not asthma severity per se
Intubation is a last resort in asthma because ventilation of hyperinflated lungs is very hazardous
explanation.pearls: Salbutamol lactate is a real trap - the rising lactate in ongoing severe asthma is often the drug, not the sepsis, and stepping to magnesium off the beta-agonist ladder is the right move.

sources.label: AMH Children's Dosing Companion: Magnesium sulfate

stem:
A 29-year-old primigravida at 34+2 weeks presents to birth suite with a headache and epigastric pain. She has been reviewed weekly for suspected pre-eclampsia and is on labetalol 200 mg orally three times daily. On arrival her observations are recorded as shown.

On examination her reflexes are brisk with no clonus, urinalysis shows 3+ protein, and CTG shows a normal foetal heart rate trace with reactive baseline. Airway is patent, breath sounds are clear, and no peripheral oedema is noted apart from mild ankle swelling.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, BP 172/112 (repeated 168/110 after 15 min), RR 20, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temp 36.6 C; foetal heart rate 148
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 118 x10^9/L (150-400); ALT 62 U/L (<30); creatinine 88 micromol/L (45-90); urate 0.42 mmol/L (<0.35); urine PCR 320 mg/mmol (<30)
data_table.Medications: Labetalol 200 mg TDS oral; iron; low-dose aspirin 150 mg nocte

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate antihypertensive?

options.text: Increase oral labetalol dose to 300 mg every 8 hours with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Oral labetalol is inadequate at this BP and pace of end-organ signs (headache, epigastric pain, transaminitis, thrombocytopenia). Waiting 60 minutes on an inadequate oral dose delays control and risks stroke. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

options.text: Sublingual nifedipine immediate release 10 mg with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Sublingual nifedipine is contraindicated in pregnancy for severe hypertension because of unpredictable BP drop and risk of foetal compromise. Oral nifedipine immediate release is the alternative when IV labetalol is contraindicated, but sublingual is not the route. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

options.text: Sodium nitroprusside infusion titrated to a MAP of 100 mmHg with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Sodium nitroprusside is reserved for refractory severe hypertension and carries risk of foetal cyanide toxicity with prolonged use; it is not a first-line agent in obstetric hypertensive emergency. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

options.text: Intravenous labetalol 20 mg over 2 minutes, repeat with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: SOMANZ guideline first-line for severe hypertension in pregnancy is IV labetalol 20 mg over 2 minutes, repeated at 15 min intervals with dose doubling to a max of 300 mg. Oral labetalol has failed to control her BP so IV is appropriate. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

options.text: Intravenous hydralazine 20 mg bolus with cardiac monitoring throughout and reassessment within 30 minutes
options.rationale: The SOMANZ hydralazine dose is 5 mg IV slowly, repeatable to 20 mg total; a 20 mg single bolus risks precipitous maternal hypotension and foetal bradycardia. IV labetalol is the SOMANZ first choice unless contraindicated. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

explanation.summary: Severe hypertension in pregnancy (systolic 160 or more, diastolic 110 or more) is a hypertensive emergency because of stroke and abruption risk. SOMANZ first-line is IV labetalol 20 mg over 2 minutes with dose doubling at 15 minute intervals up to 300 mg total. Sublingual nifedipine is contraindicated; hydralazine is second-line at 5 mg IV, not 20 mg bolus.
key_points: Severe HTN in pregnancy: IV labetalol 20 mg then double every 15 min to 300 mg max
Sublingual nifedipine is contraindicated - only oral immediate release is acceptable
Hydralazine second-line: 5 mg IV slow, not 20 mg
Pre-eclampsia with severe HTN plus end-organ signs requires simultaneous magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis
explanation.pearls: Sublingual nifedipine is the wrong answer in obstetric hypertensive emergency every time - the trap is dose route, not drug class.

stem:
A 27-year-old G2P0 with one prior first-trimester miscarriage presents at 6+2 weeks by LMP with light PV spotting and mild left iliac fossa discomfort. Serum bhCG 48 hours ago was 2400 IU/L and is now 2900 IU/L. She has no medical comorbidities and is not on any regular medication. Her reliable partner will bring her back for follow up as required.

On examination she is haemodynamically stable with mild left adnexal tenderness on bimanual examination. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus and a left tubal 22 mm heterogeneous adnexal mass with no foetal cardiac activity and no free fluid.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82, BP 118/74, RR 16, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Investigations: Serum bhCG 2900 IU/L today (was 2400 IU/L 48 h ago); Hb 128 g/L (115-165); ALT 22 U/L (<30); creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90); Rh positive
data_table.Ultrasound: Empty uterus; left tubal 22 mm heterogeneous mass; no foetal cardiac activity; no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Expectant management with weekly bhCG and outpatient review with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Expectant management requires falling bhCG on trend; her bhCG is rising (2400 to 2900) so expectant is not indicated. Persistent or rising ectopic without treatment risks rupture. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy GPS)

options.text: Single-dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg per m2 with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: This tubal ectopic meets RANZCOG methotrexate eligibility: bhCG under 5000 IU/L, mass under 3.5 cm, no foetal cardiac activity, no significant pain, no haemorrhage, reliable follow up, normal LFTs and renal function. Single-dose IM methotrexate is the correct medical management with day 4 and day 7 bhCG check and weekly to negative. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy GPS)

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingectomy of the left tube and involve senior review with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Surgical management is indicated for haemodynamic instability, rupture, contraindication to methotrexate, or when methotrexate criteria are not met (bhCG at or over 5000 IU/L, mass at or over 3.5 cm, foetal cardiac activity). She meets none of these; medical management is preferred and preserves the tube. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy GPS)

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingostomy of the left tube and involve senior review with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Salpingostomy is a tube-preserving surgical option but is not indicated when medical management with methotrexate is safe and appropriate. Both surgical routes commit to operative recovery when medical management would work. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy GPS)

options.text: Repeat transvaginal ultrasound and bhCG in 1 week without other intervention with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: One week of no intervention with a confirmed rising ectopic risks rupture within that window. The diagnosis is already established and she is a methotrexate candidate now. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy GPS)

explanation.summary: RANZCOG methotrexate criteria for tubal ectopic are: haemodynamic stability, bhCG under 5000 IU/L, adnexal mass under 3.5 cm, no foetal cardiac activity, no significant pain, no haemorrhage, no MTX contraindications (normal LFT, renal, no immunodeficiency), and reliable follow up. Single-dose IM methotrexate 50 mg per m2 with day 4 and day 7 bhCG and weekly to negative is the standard.
key_points: MTX threshold for tubal ectopic is bhCG under 5000 IU/L in the RANZCOG GPS
Other MTX criteria: mass under 3.5 cm, no FCA, no significant pain, reliable follow up, normal LFT/renal
Dose is 50 mg per m2 IM as a single dose; day 4 and day 7 bhCG expected to drop 15 percent between
Surgical if unstable, ruptured, MTX contraindicated, or criteria not met
explanation.pearls: The RANZCOG MTX cut-off is 5000 IU/L, not the older 3000 IU/L number - AU exam trap answered with the newer threshold.

stem:
A 32-year-old G3P2 delivers a 3800 g baby vaginally after a 12 hour labour with syntocinon augmentation for slow progress. Placenta is delivered spontaneously and appears complete. Estimated blood loss at 10 minutes is 1200 mL and continues at 200 mL per 5 minutes.

On abdominal examination her uterus is soft and boggy at the level of the umbilicus. She has an in-situ intravenous line, no known allergies, and her blood pressure has just dropped from 118/72 to 96/58. She has a history of chronic hypertension in her booking notes.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 96/58, RR 24, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft and boggy at umbilicus; perineum inspected with no obvious tear; placenta complete
data_table.Medications given: Oxytocin 10 units IM at delivery of anterior shoulder (active third stage); no other drugs given

lead_in: After bimanual uterine massage what pharmacological agent would you give next?

options.text: Intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes as first-line with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid is given in parallel with uterotonics in PPH within 3 hours (WOMAN trial), but it does not replace the tonic. The primary problem is uterine atony and it needs a uterotonic first. TXA is an adjunct, not a substitute. (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum haemorrhage guideline)

options.text: Intramuscular ergometrine 500 micrograms with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension because it causes marked vasoconstriction and BP rise. Her chronic hypertension makes this an unsafe choice; carboprost is the alternative uterotonic. (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum haemorrhage guideline)

options.text: Sublingual misoprostol 800 micrograms with cardiac monitoring with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Misoprostol is a third-line uterotonic in AU practice reserved for when parenteral agents are unavailable or exhausted; it has slower onset (30-60 min) than carboprost (10-15 min). RANZCOG puts parenteral agents ahead of misoprostol. (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum haemorrhage guideline)

options.text: Intramuscular carboprost 250 micrograms with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: She has active postpartum haemorrhage from uterine atony. The RANZCOG ladder after uterine massage and oxytocin bolus is ergometrine or carboprost. Carboprost is preferred here because ergometrine is contraindicated in her chronic hypertension. Carboprost 250 mcg IM can be repeated every 15 min to a max of 2 mg. (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum haemorrhage guideline)

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g over 20 minutes with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate is not a uterotonic - it is a smooth muscle relaxant used in pre-eclampsia and tocolysis. It would worsen atony and precipitate BP drop in the shocked patient. (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum haemorrhage guideline)

explanation.summary: PPH from atony is treated with mechanical measures (bimanual compression, uterine massage) plus uterotonic escalation. RANZCOG sequences oxytocin then ergometrine or carboprost then misoprostol. Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension because of vasoconstriction; carboprost is the alternative. TXA and volume resuscitation run in parallel.
key_points: PPH uterotonic ladder: oxytocin, then ergometrine or carboprost, then misoprostol
Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension and pre-eclampsia
Carboprost is contraindicated in severe asthma but is the go-to when ergometrine cannot be used
TXA 1 g IV should be given in parallel within 3 hours - it does not replace uterotonics
explanation.pearls: The tone ladder splits on comorbidity - hypertension blocks ergometrine, asthma blocks carboprost, and the safe drug depends on which contraindication applies.

stem:
A 34-year-old G2P1 at 40+3 weeks is having a spontaneous vaginal birth. The head has just delivered but has retracted against the perineum and gentle routine axial traction with the next contraction fails to deliver the anterior shoulder. The registrar is on the way and the midwife has called for help. The mother is in a supine lithotomy position.

The patient's last birth was uncomplicated. Her booking BMI was 34 and her most recent HbA1c at 26 weeks was 42 mmol/mol. The baby is estimated to weigh 4200 g on her most recent scan.

data_table.Vital signs (mother): HR 106, BP 128/78, RR 22, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temp 37.0 C
data_table.History: G2P1, term, spontaneous vaginal delivery of head 30 seconds ago; head retracting against perineum; routine axial traction failed

lead_in: What is the next appropriate manoeuvre?

options.text: Deliberate fundal pressure at the maternal umbilicus with the contraction
options.rationale: Fundal pressure is contraindicated in shoulder dystocia because it worsens shoulder impaction against the pubic symphysis and increases uterine rupture and brachial plexus injury risk. Suprapubic pressure (over the anterior shoulder) is the correct pressure, not fundal. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia guideline)

options.text: Zavanelli manoeuvre with cephalic replacement and immediate caesarean section
options.rationale: Zavanelli is a last resort when all other manoeuvres have failed; performing it as first-line abandons the standard algorithm and commits to laparotomy for a dystocia that resolves with simpler measures in most cases. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia guideline)

options.text: McRoberts manoeuvre with hyperflexion of maternal hips to the abdomen combined
options.rationale: The AU HELPERR mnemonic and RANZCOG shoulder dystocia algorithm start with H (call for help), E (evaluate for episiotomy - not always required), L (legs into McRoberts hyperflexion). McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure resolves 50 to 60 percent of shoulder dystocia and is always first. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia guideline)

options.text: Symphysiotomy of the pubic symphysis with cardiac monitoring with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Symphysiotomy is not part of standard AU shoulder dystocia management; it has been abandoned in high-resource settings because of severe maternal morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia guideline)

options.text: Delivery of the posterior arm before McRoberts with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Posterior arm delivery is an internal manoeuvre and comes after external manoeuvres (McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure) have been tried. Skipping to internal manoeuvres first raises brachial plexus injury risk unnecessarily. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia guideline)

explanation.summary: Shoulder dystocia follows the HELPERR sequence: H (help), E (episiotomy consideration), L (legs into McRoberts hyperflexion with suprapubic pressure), P (posterior arm delivery), E (enter and rotate - Rubin, Woods), R (roll to all-fours Gaskin), R (repeat or Zavanelli). McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure resolves the majority; internal manoeuvres come after external manoeuvres fail.
key_points: First external manoeuvre: McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure (resolves 50 to 60 percent)
Fundal pressure is contraindicated; suprapubic pressure only
Internal manoeuvres (posterior arm, rotation) after external manoeuvres fail
Zavanelli and symphysiotomy are last-resort and rarely used in AU practice
explanation.pearls: Fundal pressure is the exam trap - it worsens impaction, and the correct pressure is suprapubic over the anterior shoulder.

stem:
A 31-year-old G3P2 at 36+4 weeks presents in the middle of the night after a car passenger seat impact 3 hours ago. She reports continuous abdominal pain since the accident, one small gush of PV bleeding at home, and reduced foetal movements over the last hour.

On examination she is tender across the uterus with a hard tense abdomen. Speculum shows only a small amount of dark blood in the vagina. Her last morphology scan at 20 weeks documented a fundal placenta. CTG shows a foetal heart baseline of 100 with reduced variability and late decelerations.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124, BP 96/58, RR 24, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temp 36.6 C
data_table.Examination: Uterus tender and firm (Couvelaire-like); minimal external blood loss; cervix closed and soft on speculum
data_table.Investigations: Hb 96 g/L (115-165); platelets 108 x10^9/L (150-400); fibrinogen 2.6 g/L (4.0-6.0 in pregnancy); INR 1.4 (0.9-1.2); base excess -6
data_table.CTG: Baseline 100, reduced variability, recurrent late decelerations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Cross-match blood, betamethasone 11.4 mg IM for foetal lung maturation
options.rationale: Antenatal steroids are given up to 34+6 weeks; at 36+4 they are not indicated. More importantly, this foetus cannot wait 4 hours - it is compromised now. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage GPS)

options.text: Transvaginal ultrasound to exclude placenta praevia before proceeding
options.rationale: Her 20 week morphology already documented a fundal placenta, and TV ultrasound is time consuming in a category 1 situation. Ultrasound is also poorly sensitive for abruption; delaying delivery for imaging in a compromised foetus worsens outcome. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage GPS)

options.text: Induction of labour with prostaglandin E2 gel and continuous CTG
options.rationale: Foetal bradycardia with late decelerations plus maternal DIC do not permit induction; there is no time and the CTG demands immediate delivery. Prostaglandin is contraindicated in this pattern. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage GPS)

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection and observe for 30 minutes
options.rationale: Magnesium neuroprotection is used before very preterm birth (under 30 weeks) and does not apply at 36+4. Observation for 30 minutes with foetal bradycardia and late decelerations delays delivery beyond the safe window. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage GPS)

options.text: Category 1 emergency caesarean section with major haemorrhage protocol activation
options.rationale: This is placental abruption with foetal compromise (late decelerations, bradycardia) and evolving maternal DIC (falling fibrinogen, rising INR, thrombocytopenia). RANZCOG mandates category 1 caesarean (delivery within 30 minutes) with major haemorrhage protocol activation because both mother and baby are in extremis. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage GPS)

explanation.summary: Placental abruption after trauma classically presents with continuous abdominal pain, tender rigid uterus and disproportionately small external bleeding for the clinical picture (concealed haemorrhage). Foetal compromise plus maternal coagulopathy (low fibrinogen, high INR, thrombocytopenia) is a category 1 caesarean indication with major haemorrhage protocol activation.
key_points: Concealed abruption presents with pain and firm uterus but minimal external blood
Foetal bradycardia plus late decelerations plus maternal coagulopathy = category 1 caesarean
Category 1 timing target: delivery within 30 minutes of decision
MHP activation goes in parallel because DIC is already developing
explanation.pearls: The exam trap in abruption is doing an ultrasound to exclude praevia - the CTG has already made the call, and delay costs the baby.

sources.label: RANZCOG Category of urgency for caesarean statement

stem:
A 24-year-old G1P0 at 33+1 weeks with severe pre-eclampsia is on a magnesium sulfate infusion at 1 g per hour after a 4 g loading dose 3 hours ago. The bedside nurse calls you because she has become drowsy and complains of feeling weak.

On examination she is drowsy but rousable. She has a normal blood pressure of 148/94 on labetalol infusion. Her patellar reflexes are absent bilaterally. Respiratory examination shows shallow breathing. She has an in-dwelling urinary catheter with 15 mL of urine in the last hour. Her booking creatinine was 68 micromol/L; today's is 128 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 66, BP 148/94, RR 8, SpO2 92 percent on 2 L nasal prongs, temp 36.4 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, weak, patellar reflexes absent bilaterally; shallow respiratory pattern
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 128 micromol/L (was 68 at booking); serum magnesium level pending; urine output 15 mL in last hour
data_table.Medications: Magnesium sulfate infusion 1 g per hour (loading 4 g given 3 h ago); labetalol infusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Continue magnesium at the same rate and add furosemide 40 mg IV to increase renal clearance
options.rationale: Continuing magnesium in the face of overt toxicity worsens respiratory depression and risks arrest. Furosemide is not the immediate rescue; magnesium must be stopped and calcium gluconate given first. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

options.text: Stop the magnesium sulfate infusion and give calcium gluconate 1 g intravenously over 10 minutes
options.rationale: This is magnesium toxicity with the classical sequence of loss of deep tendon reflexes then respiratory depression. Her rising creatinine and low urine output have caused magnesium accumulation. Immediate management is to stop the infusion and give calcium gluconate 1 g IV over 10 minutes as the specific antidote. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

options.text: Halve the magnesium infusion to 500 mg per hour and repeat serum magnesium in 4 hours
options.rationale: Reducing the infusion without stopping is inadequate for overt clinical toxicity; loss of reflexes plus respiratory rate 8 requires immediate reversal, not dose adjustment. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

options.text: Intubation and mechanical ventilation for airway protection before further management
options.rationale: Intubation is a rescue if the respiratory depression persists after magnesium is stopped and calcium given; it is not the first action when a specific antidote is available and can restore respiratory drive within minutes. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

options.text: Naloxone 0.4 mg IV for suspected opioid depression with cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: There is no opioid in her medication list and her clinical picture (absent reflexes, weakness, respiratory depression on a magnesium infusion in AKI) is magnesium toxicity, not opioid. Naloxone would waste time. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

explanation.summary: Magnesium toxicity in pregnancy proceeds in a predictable sequence: loss of deep tendon reflexes then respiratory depression then cardiac arrest. She has accumulated magnesium because of oliguria (15 mL in the last hour) and rising creatinine. The specific reversal is stopping the infusion and giving IV calcium gluconate 1 g over 10 minutes. Monitor urine output and reflexes hourly, keep magnesium infusion at 0.5-1 g per hour, and reduce dose in renal impairment.
key_points: Magnesium toxicity sequence: reflex loss, respiratory depression, arrest
Renal impairment or oliguria (under 30 mL per hour) accumulates magnesium rapidly
Antidote is calcium gluconate 1 g IV over 10 min
Reduce infusion rate to 0.5 g per hour in renal impairment or reduced urine output
explanation.pearls: The safety net for magnesium is reflexes and urine output at the bedside - a nurse's reflex check every hour catches toxicity before the respiratory rate drops.

stem:
A 33-year-old G4P3 at 39+4 weeks has an artificial rupture of membranes for augmentation of established labour. Two minutes later she becomes restless, complains of feeling short of breath, then loses consciousness. Foetal heart rate drops to 60.

When you arrive her airway is patent with agonal respirations, there are no palpable peripheral pulses, and she has begun to bleed briskly from her IV cannulation site and around her mouth. The senior midwife has called an obstetric emergency and started chest compressions.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 40 (transitioned from 118 in 60 seconds), BP unrecordable, SpO2 84 percent on 15 L non-rebreather, RR agonal, temp 36.8 C
data_table.Recent events: ARM 2 minutes ago; sudden collapse; brisk oozing from IV site and gums; foetal heart 60
data_table.Investigations: Bedside ROTEM pending; venous blood gas being drawn

lead_in: What is the single most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Anaphylaxis to intravenous oxytocin with cardiac monitoring throughout and reassessment within 30 minutes
options.rationale: Oxytocin anaphylaxis is very rare and typically produces urticarial rash, bronchospasm and hypotension without immediate DIC. There is no rash description here and the bleeding pattern does not match anaphylaxis. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines 2023)

options.text: Pulmonary embolism from thrombus with cardiac monitoring throughout and reassessment within 30 minutes
options.rationale: Pulmonary thromboembolism causes acute hypoxia and haemodynamic collapse but does not produce simultaneous rapid-onset consumptive coagulopathy from IV and gum bleeding within minutes. The DIC-like coagulopathy is the AFE fingerprint. (Source: RANZCOG Amniotic fluid embolism statement)

options.text: Eclampsia with seizure and hypoxia with cardiac monitoring throughout and reassessment within 30 minutes
options.rationale: Eclampsia usually presents with a tonic-clonic seizure and post-ictal state, not the immediate coagulopathic bleeding pattern here. There is no BP surge history and the coagulopathy pattern does not fit eclampsia. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

options.text: Uterine rupture with cardiac monitoring throughout and reassessment within 30 minutes
options.rationale: Uterine rupture in a G4P3 without a scarred uterus is possible but typically presents with abdominal pain, tenderness, loss of foetal station, and haemorrhagic shock without such rapid-onset consumptive coagulopathy. The temporal link to ARM and the mucosal oozing point elsewhere. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage GPS)

options.text: Amniotic fluid embolism with cardiac monitoring throughout and reassessment within 30 minutes
options.rationale: The triad of sudden cardiovascular collapse, hypoxaemia and consumptive coagulopathy (oozing from puncture sites and mucous membranes) at the time of ARM or delivery is classical for amniotic fluid embolism (AFE). Diagnosis is clinical; treatment is supportive with immediate resuscitative caesarean if maternal arrest, massive transfusion protocol and ICU. (Source: RANZCOG Amniotic fluid embolism statement)

explanation.summary: AFE is characterised by sudden cardiovascular collapse, hypoxaemia and coagulopathy occurring during labour, at ARM or delivery, or immediately postpartum. It is a clinical diagnosis; there is no bedside test. Management is supportive - airway, oxygen, resuscitative caesarean within 4 minutes of maternal arrest, MHP activation, ICU. Mortality remains high despite treatment.
key_points: AFE triad: sudden cardiovascular collapse, hypoxaemia, DIC
Temporal association with ARM, delivery, or immediate postpartum
Diagnosis is clinical; ROTEM will show consumptive coagulopathy but does not confirm AFE
Perimortem caesarean within 4 minutes of maternal arrest if not already delivered
explanation.pearls: The AFE fingerprint is coagulopathy with bleeding from IV sites and mucous membranes appearing within minutes - PE does not do that.

stem:
A 32-year-old G3P0 with a prior right tubal ectopic managed by right salpingectomy 3 years ago presents with 4 hours of severe left iliac fossa pain and syncope. Her serum bhCG is 8200 IU/L today. She was trying to conceive after unsuccessful IVF cycles and this is a spontaneous pregnancy.

On examination she has a distended tender abdomen with guarding and rebound in the left iliac fossa. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus, a left tubal 32 mm mass with foetal cardiac activity, and significant free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. She is now peripherally shut down.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 84/56, RR 26, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temp 36.5 C
data_table.Examination: Peripherally shut down; peritonism left iliac fossa; guarding and rebound
data_table.Investigations: Serum bhCG 8200 IU/L; Hb 88 g/L (115-165) (was 128 last week); group and screen underway; Rh positive
data_table.Ultrasound: Empty uterus; left tubal 32 mm mass with foetal cardiac activity; large volume free fluid in the pouch of Douglas
data_table.History: Prior right salpingectomy for ectopic 3 years ago; nil other surgical history; failed IVF cycles

lead_in: What is the most appropriate surgical management now?

options.text: Uterine artery embolisation in interventional radiology to control bleeding
options.rationale: UAE is used for postpartum haemorrhage refractory to medical management, arteriovenous malformations, and specific fibroid indications; it is not the treatment for ruptured tubal ectopic. Definitive surgical removal is required. (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum haemorrhage guideline)

options.text: Emergency laparoscopic left salpingostomy to preserve the only remaining tube
options.rationale: Salpingostomy is contraindicated in haemodynamic instability and in ruptured ectopic because it is technically slower, has 5 to 15 percent persistent trophoblast rate requiring MTX follow up, and same-tube recurrence approaches 20 percent - the very tube she is trying to preserve is now maximally damaged. IVF is her fertility pathway. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy GPS)

options.text: Intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg per m2 and admission for observation
options.rationale: MTX is contraindicated in haemodynamic instability, rupture, foetal cardiac activity, mass over 3.5 cm, and bhCG at or over 5000 IU/L. She fails all five of these criteria. MTX would delay definitive surgical control of bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy GPS)

options.text: Emergency laparoscopic left salpingectomy after major haemorrhage protocol activation
options.rationale: She has a ruptured left tubal ectopic with shock in her only remaining tube. Although salpingostomy might otherwise be preferred to preserve the only remaining tube, the RANZCOG evidence base shows salpingostomy has a 5 to 15 percent persistent trophoblast rate and 15 to 20 percent recurrent same-tube ectopic rate. In a haemodynamically unstable patient with a large ruptured mass, salpingectomy is safer and definitive; future fertility can be pursued via IVF. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy GPS)

options.text: Cross-match, resuscitate, and re-scan in 6 hours before deciding surgery
options.rationale: She has already ruptured and is shocked; the diagnosis is made and the operating theatre needs her now. Waiting 6 hours risks exsanguination. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy GPS)

explanation.summary: This T14-flip scenario tests the historical-bilaterality inversion: the standard teaching that a prior contralateral salpingectomy should push you toward salpingostomy to preserve the only remaining tube is over-ruled by haemodynamic instability, rupture, mass over 3.5 cm, foetal cardiac activity and bhCG well above the MTX threshold. In this real-world constellation salpingectomy is safer, definitive, and IVF becomes her fertility route.
key_points: MTX absolute contraindications include instability, rupture, FCA, mass over 3.5 cm, bhCG at or over 5000 IU/L
Salpingostomy has 5 to 15 percent persistent trophoblast and 15 to 20 percent recurrent same-tube ectopic
Haemodynamic instability trumps tube-preservation logic - salpingectomy is safer
Fertility via IVF is a legitimate downstream plan when both tubes are lost
explanation.pearls: The historical-bilaterality flip usually favours preservation, but rupture with instability inverts it back to salpingectomy - safety over sentiment.

stem:
A 24-year-old woman is brought to your ED by ambulance one hour after taking her partner's amitriptyline in a suicide attempt. She reports taking about 30 tablets of 25 mg each. She was found drowsy but rousable at home.

On arrival she is drowsy with GCS 12, has warm dry skin, and dilated poorly reactive pupils. Her bladder is distended and there are no bowel sounds. ECG shows a broad QRS with a terminal R wave in aVR.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128 sinus tachycardia, BP 96/58, RR 16, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temp 37.2 C
data_table.Examination: GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5); pupils dilated 6 mm and poorly reactive; skin warm dry; bladder distended
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.30, HCO3 18 mmol/L, lactate 2.6 mmol/L; potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); paracetamol level negative
data_table.ECG: Sinus tachycardia, QRS 148 ms, terminal R wave in aVR height 4 mm, QTc 512 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Activated charcoal 50 g nasogastric with airway protection with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Charcoal is used within 1 to 2 hours of a potentially toxic ingestion if the airway is protected, but it is an adjunct - it does not treat the sodium channel blockade already causing QRS widening. Bicarbonate is the immediate life-saving intervention. (Source: eTG complete: TCA poisoning)

options.text: Intravenous physostigmine 2 mg over 5 minutes for reversal of anticholinergic toxicity
options.rationale: Physostigmine is contraindicated in TCA overdose because it can precipitate seizure, bradyarrhythmia and asystole in the context of sodium channel blockade. It is used in pure anticholinergic toxidrome without cardiac conduction disturbance. (Source: eTG complete: Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning)

options.text: Sodium bicarbonate 8.4 percent 100 mL intravenous bolus with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: QRS over 100 ms and terminal R wave in aVR over 3 mm are markers of TCA sodium channel blockade with risk of ventricular arrhythmia and seizure. Sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol per kg IV bolus (roughly 100 mL of 8.4 percent) is antidotal and repeated to a target pH 7.50 to 7.55, with QRS narrowing as the endpoint. (Source: eTG complete: Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning)

options.text: Flumazenil 0.2 mg IV titrated to arousal and repeat as clinically indicated
options.rationale: Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist and is not indicated in TCA overdose - it would not treat toxicity and risks precipitating seizure in mixed overdoses. (Source: eTG complete: Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning)

options.text: Amiodarone 300 mg IV infusion for the broad complex tachycardia with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Class III antiarrhythmics are contraindicated because they prolong QT and worsen conduction; class Ia and Ic are also contraindicated. Sodium bicarbonate is both antidotal and the correct rhythm treatment for TCA-induced wide complex tachycardia. (Source: eTG complete: Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning)

explanation.summary: TCA overdose causes an anticholinergic toxidrome plus fast-sodium channel blockade producing QRS widening, aVR terminal R wave over 3 mm, seizure, hypotension and ventricular arrhythmia. Sodium bicarbonate is the antidote because it narrows QRS by increasing extracellular sodium and pH-dependent unbinding from the sodium channel. Target pH 7.50 to 7.55 titrated to QRS narrowing.
key_points: QRS over 100 ms or aVR terminal R over 3 mm predicts seizure and VT
Bicarbonate 1-2 mmol per kg IV bolus then infusion to pH 7.50 to 7.55
Physostigmine and class I/III antiarrhythmics are contraindicated
Charcoal within 1-2 hours only after airway protection; not a substitute for bicarbonate
explanation.pearls: The aVR terminal R wave over 3 mm is the QRS-independent marker that flips the case to bicarbonate before the QRS reaches 100 ms.

stem:
A 52-year-old man with stable schizophrenia on olanzapine 15 mg nocte for the past 4 years attends your general practice wanting to stop smoking. He smokes 25 cigarettes per day and has smoked for 30 years. He has tried to quit unassisted twice, each time relapsing within 2 weeks. He has no history of severe depression, no active suicidal ideation, and his last psychiatric review documented stable mood.

He has hypertension well controlled on perindopril, no history of seizures, and no cardiovascular events. His Fagerstrom Test for Nicotine Dependence score is 7 of 10 (high).

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82, BP 132/78, RR 16, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temp 36.6 C
data_table.Investigations: HbA1c 39 mmol/mol (<42); LDL 3.6 mmol/L; creatinine 78 micromol/L (60-110)
data_table.Medications: Olanzapine 15 mg nocte; perindopril 5 mg mane; no other regular medication

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Varenicline 0.5 mg daily titrating to 1 mg twice daily with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Varenicline is first-line for heavy smokers with high nicotine dependence per the RACGP guideline; it has the strongest quit rate at 12 weeks compared with NRT and bupropion. Prior concerns about neuropsychiatric adverse effects have been largely reassured by the EAGLES trial including in patients with stable psychiatric illness. Titration and early review are standard. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation guideline 2019)

options.text: Bupropion sustained release 150 mg daily for 3 days then 150 mg twice daily with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Bupropion is second-line and is contraindicated or requires caution in patients with seizure risk, eating disorders, and MAOI use; olanzapine is not a contraindication but bupropion is less effective than varenicline as first-line in heavy dependence. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation guideline 2019)

options.text: Nicotine replacement patch 21 mg daily monotherapy without oral NRT top up with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Combination NRT (patch plus short-acting oral form) is more effective than monotherapy for heavy smokers; patch alone is inadequate at FTND 7. Varenicline still has the strongest evidence at this level of dependence. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation guideline 2019)

options.text: Nicotine vaping product first-line before other pharmacotherapy with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Nicotine vaping is second-line in the RACGP guideline reserved for patients who have failed or cannot tolerate approved pharmacotherapy (varenicline, NRT, bupropion). Regulatory access under prescription applies since 2024. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation guideline 2019)

options.text: Behavioural counselling only with no pharmacotherapy given his psychiatric history with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Behavioural intervention combined with pharmacotherapy has superior quit rates versus behavioural alone. Stable schizophrenia is not a contraindication to varenicline; withholding pharmacotherapy on that basis is under-treatment. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation guideline 2019)

explanation.summary: For a heavily dependent smoker (FTND 7 of 10) with stable schizophrenia, varenicline is first-line per RACGP because it has the highest cessation rate. EAGLES supports its safety in stable psychiatric illness. Behavioural support runs in parallel. Second-line agents are combination NRT and bupropion; nicotine vaping is reserved for those who fail approved pharmacotherapy.
key_points: Varenicline first-line for heavy dependence per RACGP
EAGLES trial reassures neuropsychiatric safety in stable psychiatric illness
Combination NRT (patch + short-acting) beats patch monotherapy at high dependence
Nicotine vaping is second-line, prescription only in AU
explanation.pearls: Stable schizophrenia is not a contraindication to varenicline - the historical black-box concern was diluted by EAGLES.

stem:
You are a psychiatry registrar reviewing a 15-year-old girl brought by her parents to a specialist eating disorders clinic. She has lost 12 kg over 6 months to a BMI of 15.4. Blood pressure is 88/56 supine and drops to 68/44 on standing; heart rate is 44 bpm at rest. She meets DSM-5 criteria for anorexia nervosa, restrictive subtype.

Her parents are supportive but exhausted. She lives with both parents and a 12 year old brother. Her physical status is medically stable enough for outpatient management by the eating disorder physician who is co-managing her. She has no comorbid depression or suicidality that requires acute admission.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 44 sinus bradycardia, BP 88/56 supine (68/44 standing), RR 16, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temp 36.1 C
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); phosphate 0.8 mmol/L (0.8-1.5); LFTs mildly elevated; ECG QTc 452 ms
data_table.History: Bradycardia and orthostasis but medically manageable outpatient with weekly medical review; no comorbid depression; family intact and engaged

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line psychological intervention?

options.text: Family Based Therapy (FBT / Maudsley) with parents taking initial control of refeeding
options.rationale: For adolescents with anorexia nervosa who are medically stable enough for outpatient care, FBT (Maudsley model) is the first-line psychological therapy per RANZCP Australian and NEDC guidelines. Parents take control of refeeding in phase 1, with staged transfer of control back to the adolescent through phases 2 and 3. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Eating Disorders 2023)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Eating Disorders 2023

options.text: Individual cognitive behavioural therapy for eating disorders (CBT-E) as first-line for this age
options.rationale: CBT-E is first-line for adults with eating disorders and is an alternative for adolescents where FBT is unavailable or unsuitable; in adolescents FBT has stronger evidence and is first-line per RANZCP. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Eating Disorders 2023)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Eating Disorders 2023

options.text: Interpersonal psychotherapy (IPT) as first-line with cardiac monitoring with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: IPT has some evidence in bulimia nervosa and MDD but is not first-line for anorexia in adolescents; FBT has the strongest evidence base in this age group. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Eating Disorders 2023)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Eating Disorders 2023

options.text: Fluoxetine 20 mg daily as first-line to treat the underlying anxiety and improve intake
options.rationale: SSRIs do not improve weight restoration or core anorexia symptoms in the acutely underweight state; they are considered only for persistent comorbid depression or anxiety after weight restoration. Fluoxetine is first-line for bulimia, not anorexia. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Eating Disorders 2023)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Eating Disorders 2023

options.text: Olanzapine 2.5 mg nocte for weight gain and reduction of anorexic cognitions with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Olanzapine has modest evidence for weight gain in adults with severe anorexia but is not first-line psychological or pharmacological therapy in adolescents. It is not recommended by RANZCP as a first-line intervention. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Eating Disorders 2023)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Eating Disorders 2023

explanation.summary: For medically stable adolescents with anorexia nervosa, FBT (Maudsley model) is the first-line psychological intervention in AU per RANZCP and NEDC. FBT has three phases: parents take control of refeeding, staged handover of control, and adolescent development. CBT-E is the adult first-line and an adolescent alternative when FBT is not feasible. Medication has no first-line role in anorexia.
key_points: Adolescent anorexia first-line psychological therapy is FBT
Adult anorexia first-line is CBT-E, MANTRA, or SSCM
SSRIs do not restore weight in acute anorexia - reserve for persistent post-restoration depression
Refeeding syndrome risk requires phosphate, magnesium, potassium and thiamine monitoring
explanation.pearls: FBT is the AU first-line for adolescent anorexia when the parents are able to take charge of refeeding - do not default to individual CBT in this age group.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Eating Disorders 2023
NEDC National Eating Disorders Collaboration guidelines

stem:
A 22-year-old man is brought in by friends after taking a tablet at a music festival 3 hours ago. He has been sweating profusely, has drunk 3 to 4 litres of water in the last 90 minutes, and now looks confused. His last regular medication is escitalopram 10 mg daily for anxiety.

On examination he is agitated, has hyperreflexia and inducible clonus at both ankles, and pupils are dilated. His skin is diaphoretic and warm. Bowel sounds are hyperactive. There is no focal neurology. He is oriented to person only.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132, BP 158/98, RR 24, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temp 39.6 C
data_table.Examination: Agitated, confused; hyperreflexia lower more than upper limbs; inducible clonus both ankles; pupils dilated; diaphoretic; hyperactive bowel sounds
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 122 mmol/L (135-145); potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); creatinine 132 micromol/L (60-110); CK 4200 U/L (<200); glucose 5.8 mmol/L; venous ammonia not indicated

lead_in: Which single treatment addresses the most urgent life threat first?

options.text: Hypertonic 3 percent sodium chloride 150 mL over 15 minutes with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: The most urgent life threat is severe hyponatraemia (Na 122 mmol/L) with encephalopathy from MDMA-induced SIADH and free water excess, at risk of cerebral oedema and seizure. eTG poisoning guidance for symptomatic hyponatraemia after MDMA is 3 percent saline 150 mL IV over 15 min, repeatable to a total sodium rise of 4-6 mmol/L in the first hour. Cyproheptadine and dantrolene address serotonin syndrome and hyperthermia but the sodium is the immediate killer. (Source: eTG complete: Amphetamine toxicity)

options.text: Cyproheptadine 12 mg oral single dose for serotonin syndrome with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Cyproheptadine is an adjunct in serotonin syndrome but does not address the acute cerebral oedema from severe hyponatraemia which is the immediate life threat here. It also cannot be given orally to a confused patient safely. (Source: eTG complete: Serotonin syndrome)

options.text: Dantrolene 2.5 mg per kg IV for hyperthermia with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Dantrolene is used in malignant hyperthermia and severe MDMA-related hyperthermia (over 39.5 C refractory to cooling); active external cooling, benzodiazepines and paralysis-plus-intubation are first-line and the hyponatraemia takes priority. (Source: eTG complete: Amphetamine toxicity)

options.text: Activated charcoal 50 g nasogastric with airway protection with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Charcoal is not indicated 3 hours after MDMA ingestion in a confused patient without airway protection; adsorbent decontamination will not fix the sodium of 122 mmol/L. (Source: eTG complete: Amphetamine toxicity)

options.text: Bromocriptine 2.5 mg orally for suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome
options.rationale: This is not NMS - the trigger is a serotonergic drug (MDMA plus SSRI), not a dopamine antagonist. Bromocriptine has no evidence in serotonin syndrome and is not the immediate life-saving intervention. (Source: eTG complete: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome)

explanation.summary: MDMA plus SSRI creates a mixed picture: serotonin syndrome (hyperreflexia, clonus, hyperthermia, agitation, diaphoresis, hyperactive bowel sounds), plus SIADH with excess water intake causing dilutional hyponatraemia. In festival goers this hyponatraemia with encephalopathy is the leading cause of death and must be corrected first with hypertonic saline. Cooling, benzodiazepines and supportive care follow.
key_points: MDMA hyponatraemia is dilutional plus SIADH plus water intake - encephalopathy is the killer
