Symptomatic hyponatraemia: 3 percent saline 150 mL IV over 15 min, repeatable to Na rise 4-6 mmol/L
Serotonin syndrome features - hyperreflexia, clonus, autonomic instability - present but not the immediate lethal issue here
Cyproheptadine and dantrolene are adjuncts, not first-line rescue
explanation.pearls: In an MDMA festival collapse, always check the sodium before you chase serotonin syndrome - dilutional hyponatraemia kills faster than clonus.

stem:
A 20-year-old university student is brought to your community mental health service by his parents after 5 weeks of paranoid delusions that a lecturer is broadcasting his thoughts, and third person auditory hallucinations. He has been smoking high-potency cannabis daily for 3 months at increasing dose.

He has one prior week-long episode of similar symptoms 6 months ago that self-resolved within 5 days of stopping cannabis. Family history is negative for psychotic illness. He has no depression, no mania, and is medically well. His urine drug screen is positive for cannabis and negative for methamphetamine.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 84, BP 122/74, RR 16, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen positive for THC, negative for methamphetamine, amphetamines, MDMA, cocaine; TFTs normal; CT head normal; syphilis serology negative
data_table.History: Daily high-potency cannabis for 3 months; prior 1 week self-limiting episode 6 months ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial diagnostic formulation and management?

options.text: Schizophreniform disorder; commence aripiprazole and re-evaluate at 6 months
options.rationale: Schizophreniform requires 1 to 6 months of characteristic symptoms without full schizophrenia criteria. It is a possible differential but the temporal link to cannabis and prior resolution with cessation make cannabis-induced disorder the primary formulation now. (Source: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: First-episode schizophrenia; commence olanzapine 10 mg nocte with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Schizophrenia diagnosis requires 6 months of active plus prodromal symptoms per DSM-5. His duration is 5 weeks with a temporally linked substance use and a prior episode that resolved with cessation. Premature schizophrenia labelling exposes him to indefinite antipsychotic treatment. (Source: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder; short course of oral risperidone 1 to 2 mg daily
options.rationale: DSM-5 cannabis-induced psychotic disorder is diagnosed when psychotic symptoms develop during or shortly after intoxication, exceed the expected effects of intoxication, and are not better explained by a primary psychotic disorder. Weekly progression across substance use, prior self-resolving episode with cessation, and negative family history support this over primary schizophrenia. Short course low-dose antipsychotic plus cessation support is standard; a diagnosis of schizophrenia requires 6 months of active plus prodromal features per DSM-5. (Source: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: Brief psychotic disorder; observe without medication for 4 weeks with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Brief psychotic disorder requires less than 1 month duration; he is at 5 weeks so it does not fit. Observing without treatment for actively delusional symptoms with hallucinations is under-treatment; his agitation and delusions warrant a brief antipsychotic course. (Source: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: Delusional disorder; commence pimozide and cognitive therapy with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Delusional disorder requires non-bizarre delusions without prominent hallucinations for at least 1 month, and functioning is largely preserved. His third-person auditory hallucinations and cannabis link do not fit. Pimozide is rarely used in AU practice. (Source: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders

explanation.summary: Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder is diagnosed when psychotic symptoms develop during or shortly after cannabis use, exceed intoxication effects, and cannot be better explained by a primary psychotic disorder. About 40-50 percent of cannabis-induced psychosis progresses to schizophrenia within 8 years, so structured follow up is critical, but the initial label should be substance-induced when the pattern fits. Short course low-dose antipsychotic plus cessation is the current standard.
key_points: Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder: temporal link, exceeds intoxication, not better explained by primary
Schizophrenia requires 6 months of active plus prodromal features
40-50 percent conversion to schizophrenia within 8 years - structured follow up mandatory
Short course low-dose antipsychotic plus cessation is the standard first step
explanation.pearls: Do not label schizophrenia at 5 weeks with a temporally linked substance and prior self-resolving episode - the diagnosis matters for prognosis and prescribing years ahead.

sources.label: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders
DSM-5-TR criteria for substance-induced psychotic disorder

stem:
A 34-year-old man with a documented history of two prior manic episodes with psychotic features is admitted with 8 weeks of persecutory delusions and third person auditory hallucinations that persist despite his mood being euthymic for the last 3 weeks after starting olanzapine and lithium. He has never had persistent psychotic symptoms outside of a mood episode until now.

His last manic episode was 4 months ago and remitted after admission and pharmacotherapy. His mood has been fully euthymic for the past 3 weeks with adherence confirmed by drug levels. There is no substance use on toxicology screening.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76, BP 122/78, RR 16, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temp 36.5 C
data_table.Investigations: Serum lithium 0.7 mmol/L (0.6-1.0); TFTs normal; urine drug screen negative; CT head normal
data_table.Mental state: Mood euthymic for 3 weeks; delusions of persecution and third-person auditory hallucinations persistent
data_table.Medications: Olanzapine 15 mg nocte; lithium 900 mg nocte

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis based on the current pattern?

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: DSM-5 schizoaffective disorder requires an uninterrupted period of illness with a major mood episode plus criterion A for schizophrenia, AND delusions or hallucinations for at least 2 weeks in the absence of a major mood episode, AND mood symptoms present for most of the total illness. Persistence of hallucinations and delusions for 3 weeks after mood remission fits the mood-independent psychosis criterion. Bipolar type is specified because his mood episodes have included mania. (Source: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Bipolar I with mood-congruent or incongruent psychotic features requires that the psychotic symptoms are confined to mood episodes. Persistence for 3 weeks after mood remission takes the diagnosis out of bipolar I with psychotic features and into schizoaffective. (Source: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: Schizophrenia comorbid with bipolar I disorder with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: DSM-5 does not combine schizophrenia with bipolar disorder as separate diagnoses when the pattern meets schizoaffective criteria. Schizoaffective is the single diagnosis that captures both mood and psychotic components across time. (Source: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: Delusional disorder and involve senior review with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Delusional disorder requires non-bizarre delusions without prominent hallucinations for at least 1 month and largely preserved functioning; his auditory hallucinations and mood episode history rule this out. (Source: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: Persistent psychotic disorder due to another medical condition
options.rationale: There is no medical cause on investigation (normal TFTs, CT, negative drug screen) and the pattern is fully explained by the psychiatric diagnosis of schizoaffective disorder. Attributing to a medical cause without evidence is speculative. (Source: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders

explanation.summary: The hinge that shifts a bipolar with psychotic features label to schizoaffective is at least 2 weeks of psychotic symptoms outside a mood episode within the illness course. Here delusions and hallucinations have persisted 3 weeks into euthymic mood, meeting the DSM-5 criterion. Bipolar type is specified because his mood episodes have included mania. Management combines antipsychotic and mood stabiliser long-term.
key_points: Schizoaffective criterion: at least 2 weeks of psychosis without a major mood episode within the illness
Bipolar type specified when mania has been present at any time
Bipolar I with psychotic features requires psychosis to be confined to mood episodes
Management typically combines antipsychotic with mood stabiliser or antidepressant depending on subtype
explanation.pearls: The 2-week rule for mood-independent psychosis is the DSM-5 hinge that flips bipolar with psychosis over to schizoaffective.

sources.label: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders

stem:
A 27-year-old man is brought in by ambulance from a nightclub at 3 am after being found unresponsive on the dance floor. Friends report he had a small dose of a clear liquid drink from a friend about 40 minutes ago and appeared normal until sudden collapse. He has no known medical history and is not on regular medication.

On arrival he responds to painful stimulus only. Airway is patent and self-maintained. Pupils are 3 mm and reactive. There is no track marks. Ambulance report saline 500 mL infused en route. His symptoms are already improving within 20 minutes of ED arrival.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 52, BP 108/64, RR 14, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temp 36.4 C
data_table.Examination: GCS 8 (E2 V2 M4) on arrival, improving to E3 V4 M5 within 20 minutes; pupils 3 mm and reactive; no track marks
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 4.8 mmol/L; VBG pH 7.36, HCO3 24 mmol/L; ethanol level 0.02 percent (0.020 g per 100 mL); paracetamol negative; salicylate negative

lead_in: What is the most likely toxin and appropriate management?

options.text: Ethanol toxicity - fluids, thiamine, and monitor for withdrawal with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: His ethanol level is only 0.02 percent which cannot account for GCS 8; ethanol toxicity at this level does not cause coma. The rapid onset and offset pattern is inconsistent with ethanol. (Source: eTG complete: Alcohol intoxication)

options.text: Opioid overdose - naloxone 0.4 mg IV titrated to respiratory rate over 12 with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Opioids typically cause pinpoint pupils (not 3 mm reactive), respiratory depression rather than bradycardia as the earliest finding, and do not spontaneously resolve within 20 to 40 minutes. Naloxone will fail to reverse GHB and would waste time. (Source: eTG complete: Opioid poisoning)

options.text: Benzodiazepine overdose - flumazenil 0.2 mg IV titrated to arousal with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated in overdose of unknown ingestion because it can precipitate seizures in mixed overdoses (particularly TCA or chronic benzo use). Benzodiazepine coma also does not typically cause this degree of rapid emergence. (Source: eTG complete: Benzodiazepine poisoning)

options.text: Gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB) toxicity - supportive care with airway protection with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: The GHB pattern is rapid-onset coma from a clear liquid drink 40 minutes prior, bradycardia (typical of GHB), preserved airway reflexes with pupillary reactivity and minimal ethanol, and characteristic rapid emergence in 20 to 40 minutes. There is no specific antidote; supportive care with airway protection and monitoring is standard; naloxone and flumazenil are ineffective. (Source: eTG complete: GHB toxicity)

options.text: Ketamine toxicity - benzodiazepines for agitation on emergence, no specific antidote with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Ketamine typically produces dissociative agitation, nystagmus, hypersalivation, tachycardia and hypertension, not bradycardia and unresponsiveness. His clinical pattern does not fit ketamine. (Source: eTG complete: Ketamine)

explanation.summary: GHB overdose is characterised by rapid-onset coma from a small volume of clear liquid, bradycardia and hypothermia, preserved airway reflexes, and rapid spontaneous emergence within 20 to 40 minutes. There is no antidote; supportive care with airway protection and cardiac monitoring is standard. Do not use naloxone or flumazenil - both waste time and flumazenil can be harmful in mixed overdose.
key_points: GHB coma is typically rapid onset and offset within 20 to 40 minutes
Bradycardia and hypothermia are typical; pupils remain reactive
No antidote - supportive care with airway protection
Naloxone and flumazenil are not indicated; flumazenil may be harmful
explanation.pearls: The GHB fingerprint is rapid coma to rapid recovery from a small volume clear liquid, with reactive pupils and bradycardia - naloxone tempts you but is the wrong reflex.

subtopic_detail: Warfarin reversal high INR no bleed
stem:
A 68-year-old man on warfarin for a mechanical mitral valve presents with a routine INR check showing 8.4. He has no bleeding, no bruising, and reports no recent medication changes but did complete a 5 day course of clarithromycin last week for a chest infection. His last INR 3 weeks ago was 2.6.

He is haemodynamically stable and fully asymptomatic. His usual warfarin dose is 4 mg daily. There is no easy bruising on skin examination, no gastrointestinal bleeding, and no haematuria.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78, BP 138/82, RR 14, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temp 36.6 C
data_table.Investigations: INR 8.4 today (was 2.6 three weeks ago); Hb 138 g/L (130-170); platelets 264 x10^9/L (150-400); creatinine 96 micromol/L (60-110)
data_table.Medications: Warfarin 4 mg daily; recent 5 day clarithromycin course completed last week

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.text: Withhold warfarin only and recheck INR in 24 hours without vitamin K with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: At INR over 8 without bleeding, oral vitamin K reduces bleeding risk more reliably than withholding alone, without creating warfarin resistance if the dose is kept low (1 to 2 mg). Withholding alone is used for INR 5 to 8 without bleeding. (Source: eTG complete: Warfarin reversal)

options.text: Withhold warfarin and give oral vitamin K1 (phytomenadione) 1 to 2 mg with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: For INR over 8 without bleeding, the AMH/eTG recommendation is to withhold warfarin and give low-dose oral vitamin K (1 to 2 mg) to bring INR into range within 24 hours without causing warfarin resistance. Higher doses (5 mg or more) or IV vitamin K risk over-reversal and make re-anticoagulation difficult, particularly important in mechanical valves. (Source: eTG complete: Warfarin reversal)

options.text: Withhold warfarin and give prothrombin complex concentrate (Prothrombinex-VF) 25 IU per kg IV
options.rationale: PCC is reserved for major bleeding or urgent surgical need, not asymptomatic supra-therapeutic INR. It carries thromboembolic risk which is particularly relevant in a mechanical valve. (Source: eTG complete: Warfarin reversal)

options.text: Withhold warfarin and give vitamin K1 10 mg intravenously slowly with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: IV vitamin K at 10 mg over-reverses the anticoagulation and leaves the mechanical valve unprotected; it also creates warfarin resistance for days. Reserved for major bleeding. (Source: eTG complete: Warfarin reversal)

options.text: Fresh frozen plasma 15 mL per kg intravenously over 30 minutes with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: FFP is not indicated for asymptomatic supra-therapeutic INR; it carries transfusion risks and takes hours to correct INR. Reserved for major bleeding when PCC is unavailable. (Source: eTG complete: Warfarin reversal)

explanation.summary: Warfarin reversal strategy is tiered by INR and bleeding. INR 4.5 to 10 without bleeding: withhold warfarin, consider oral vitamin K 1 to 2 mg if additional risk. INR over 10 without bleeding: withhold warfarin, oral vitamin K 3 to 5 mg. Any major bleed at any INR: PCC 25 to 50 IU per kg plus IV vitamin K 5 to 10 mg. Mechanical valves require avoidance of over-reversal because sub-therapeutic INR is a stroke risk.
key_points: INR over 8 no bleeding: withhold warfarin plus oral vitamin K 1 to 2 mg
Major bleeding at any INR: PCC 25 to 50 IU per kg IV plus IV vitamin K
Avoid IV vitamin K 10 mg in mechanical valve unless bleeding - risk of over-reversal
Clarithromycin (and other macrolides) is a well-known warfarin interaction
explanation.pearls: Small oral vitamin K (1 to 2 mg) works within 24 hours without making warfarin resistant - the trap is the 10 mg IV dose that leaves a mechanical valve unprotected.

stem:
A 58-year-old man presents with 2 hours of sudden severe tearing chest pain radiating to his back and left arm. CT aortogram confirms an acute type B (descending) aortic dissection extending from just distal to the left subclavian to the infra-renal aorta. He is haemodynamically stable with no end-organ malperfusion.

On examination he has equal radial pulses, no focal neurology, and no abdominal pain. Renal function is normal, urine output preserved, and there is no leg ischaemia. He has a normal chest examination.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 178/98 (right arm) 176/96 (left arm), RR 18, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Investigations: Troponin 12 ng/L (<14); creatinine 82 micromol/L (60-110); Hb 138 g/L (130-170); D-dimer 4200 ng/mL
data_table.Imaging: CT aortogram: acute type B dissection from left subclavian to infra-renal aorta; no malperfusion; no rupture; no pericardial effusion

lead_in: What are the target heart rate and systolic blood pressure over the next 20 minutes?

options.text: Heart rate under 60 and systolic BP under 140 mmHg using metoprolol 5 mg IV single dose only
options.rationale: A single 5 mg IV bolus of metoprolol will not achieve sustained impulse control; ongoing infusion of esmolol or labetalol is required. Systolic under 140 is too permissive - the target is 100 to 120 mmHg. (Source: eTG complete: Aortic dissection)

options.text: Heart rate under 100 and systolic BP under 160 mmHg using IV GTN monotherapy
options.rationale: GTN monotherapy causes reflex tachycardia and increases dP/dt; heart rate under 100 is too permissive and misses the impulse control target that is the core physiological rationale. (Source: eTG complete: Aortic dissection)

options.text: Heart rate under 60 and systolic BP under 100 mmHg using nifedipine IR sublingual
options.rationale: Sublingual nifedipine has unpredictable BP effect and no rate control; BP under 100 systolic risks under-perfusion of dissection branch vessels. Not a first-line agent in aortic dissection. (Source: eTG complete: Aortic dissection)

options.text: No BP target - proceed straight to endovascular repair (TEVAR) with cardiac monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Uncomplicated type B dissection is managed medically; TEVAR is reserved for complicated type B (rupture, malperfusion, refractory pain, refractory hypertension despite maximal medical therapy, false lumen expansion). Bypassing medical therapy exposes to procedural risk without indication. (Source: eTG complete: Aortic dissection)

options.text: Heart rate under 60 and systolic BP 100 to 120 mmHg using IV esmolol or labetalol first
options.rationale: Acute type B dissection is managed medically with impulse control - heart rate under 60 and systolic BP 100 to 120 mmHg to reduce dP/dt (rate of pressure rise). Beta blockade is given first (esmolol or labetalol) to blunt the reflex tachycardia from vasodilators; nitroprusside or GTN is added second for residual BP. Starting with pure vasodilator alone causes reflex tachycardia and worsens shear stress. (Source: eTG complete: Aortic dissection)

explanation.summary: Acute type B aortic dissection is managed medically with rigorous impulse control - HR under 60 and SBP 100 to 120 mmHg - to reduce dP/dt and shear stress on the false lumen. Beta blockade goes first (esmolol infusion or labetalol) and vasodilator (nitroprusside or GTN) is added after rate control to avoid reflex tachycardia. TEVAR is reserved for complicated dissection.
key_points: Type B uncomplicated: medical impulse control HR under 60 and SBP 100 to 120
Beta blocker before vasodilator to avoid reflex tachycardia and increased dP/dt
TEVAR for complicated type B: rupture, malperfusion, refractory pain or BP, expansion
Type A always for surgery
explanation.pearls: The core physiology in dissection BP control is dP/dt - starting a vasodilator without a beta blocker raises shear stress even as BP drops.

stem:
A 44-year-old man is brought in by ambulance after being struck by a car. He has an obvious pelvic fracture and blood at the meatus. Prehospital he has received 1 L of crystalloid and 1 unit of O-negative packed red cells.

On arrival he is peripherally shut down with cold pale extremities. Abdomen is distended and tender. FAST scan shows free fluid in the abdomen. Ongoing bleeding is estimated at 250 mL per 5 minutes based on his chest drain and pelvic external stabiliser output. His last recorded systolic pressure was 78 despite ongoing resuscitation.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, BP 78/44, RR 32, SpO2 96 percent on non-rebreather, temp 35.2 C
data_table.Investigations: Hb 68 g/L (130-170); platelets 92 x10^9/L (150-400); INR 1.8 (0.9-1.2); fibrinogen 1.4 g/L (2-4); pH 7.18, base excess -12, lactate 9.4 mmol/L, ionised calcium 0.92 mmol/L (1.10-1.30)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Withhold platelets until count drops below 50 x10^9/L and give red cells only
options.rationale: In active haemorrhage MTP uses empiric 1:1:1 including platelets; waiting for the count to drop below 50 accepts avoidable dilutional coagulopathy and worsens outcome. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Protocol template)

options.text: Transfuse further packed red cells only until Hb is over 100, then reassess coagulation
options.rationale: Isolated red cell transfusion without FFP, platelets and cryoprecipitate creates a dilutional coagulopathy on top of the trauma-induced coagulopathy. The 1:1:1 ratio is the AU standard for major haemorrhage in trauma. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Protocol template)

options.text: Prothrombin complex concentrate (Prothrombinex-VF) 50 IU per kg IV as the first blood product
options.rationale: PCC is reserved for warfarin reversal or bleeding on DOAC (specific to factor Xa inhibitor bleeding); it is not standard in trauma-induced coagulopathy where FFP and cryoprecipitate are preferred and target multiple factor deficiencies. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Protocol template)

options.text: Activate the massive transfusion protocol with 1:1:1 packed red cells, FFP, and platelets
options.rationale: He meets ABC score and shock-index criteria for MTP activation: ongoing haemorrhage, shock, coagulopathy (INR 1.8, low fibrinogen, thrombocytopenia), acidosis and hypocalcaemia. NBA guideline for MTP is 1:1:1 red cells : FFP : platelets, with early cryoprecipitate for fibrinogen under 1.5, TXA within 3 hours of injury, and IV calcium for hypocalcaemia from citrate. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Protocol template)

options.text: Recombinant factor VIIa 90 mcg per kg IV as first-line for uncontrolled haemorrhage
options.rationale: Recombinant VIIa is a last-resort agent with thromboembolic risk; it is not first-line and never a substitute for balanced blood product resuscitation. NBA guidance restricts it to specialist decision. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Protocol template)

explanation.summary: Trauma major haemorrhage triggers MTP - 1:1:1 red cells : FFP : platelets with early cryoprecipitate for fibrinogen under 1.5, TXA 1 g IV within 3 hours (repeat at 8 h), and IV calcium for citrate-related hypocalcaemia. Isolated red cell transfusion creates dilutional coagulopathy; VIIa is a last-resort agent, not a first choice.
key_points: MTP triggers: ABC score, shock index over 1, ongoing haemorrhage, coagulopathy
Balanced ratio 1:1:1 red cells : FFP : platelets
Cryoprecipitate for fibrinogen under 1.5 g/L; TXA within 3 h
IV calcium for citrate-induced hypocalcaemia during large transfusion
explanation.pearls: Hypocalcaemia from citrate is under-recognised in massive transfusion - give calcium empirically after 4 units of blood or if ionised calcium is under 1.1.

sources.label: CRASH-2 trial for TXA in trauma

stem:
A 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents to your ED with 24 hours of pain out of proportion to physical findings in his right calf. The skin over the area looks like mild cellulitis with faint erythema. He is systemically unwell.

On examination there is faint erythema over the medial calf, exquisite tenderness on light palpation extending well beyond the area of erythema, a small area of dusky skin at the medial malleolus, and reduced sensation over the medial ankle. There is no wound of entry visible. Pedal pulses are palpable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 122, BP 96/58, RR 26, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temp 38.7 C
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.4 x10^9/L (4-11); CRP 260 mg/L (<5); sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145); glucose 16.8 mmol/L; creatinine 168 micromol/L (60-110); Hb 118 g/L (130-170); lactate 4.2 mmol/L
data_table.Imaging: Bedside soft tissue ultrasound shows fascial thickening and small gas bubbles

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: IV flucloxacillin 2 g every 6 hours and elevate the limb, review at 4 hours
options.rationale: Flucloxacillin monotherapy under-covers gram-negative and anaerobic organisms in necrotising fasciitis; waiting 4 hours delays the required surgical control that dominates mortality reduction. Cellulitis is not the diagnosis here. (Source: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections)
source_refs: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections

options.text: Urgent surgical exploration with debridement plus empirical IV meropenem plus clindamycin
options.rationale: Necrotising fasciitis requires urgent surgical debridement within 6 hours - the pain-out-of-proportion, dusky skin, reduced sensation (nerve necrosis), high LRINEC score, and fascial gas on ultrasound are all supportive. Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics per eTG include meropenem plus clindamycin (for exotoxin suppression) plus vancomycin (for MRSA cover). Antibiotics do not substitute for surgical control. (Source: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections)
source_refs: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections

options.text: IV ceftriaxone plus metronidazole and MRI to confirm before considering surgery
options.rationale: MRI delays surgery in a time-critical infection where clinical and bedside imaging findings are already diagnostic; every hour of delay increases mortality. Ceftriaxone plus metronidazole is not the AU empirical regimen for necrotising fasciitis. (Source: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections)
source_refs: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections

options.text: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy first, then antibiotics and involve senior review
options.rationale: Hyperbaric oxygen is an adjunct after surgical debridement and antibiotics have been initiated; it is not the first-line intervention and is not universally recommended. Delay for HBO would be catastrophic. (Source: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections)
source_refs: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections

options.text: Bedside incision and drainage at the point of maximal tenderness and admission for observation
options.rationale: Bedside I and D does not achieve the wide operative debridement required and may worsen sepsis by opening the plane without full source control. Definitive theatre-based debridement is mandatory. (Source: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections)
source_refs: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection kills through delay - the surgical debridement window is 6 hours. Clues that shift the diagnosis from cellulitis are pain-out-of-proportion, tenderness beyond erythema, dusky skin, sensory loss (nerve necrosis), high LRINEC, and fascial gas or fluid on imaging. Empirical antibiotics per eTG are meropenem plus clindamycin plus vancomycin.
key_points: Pain out of proportion, sensory loss, and dusky skin are the necrotising red flags
LRINEC 6 or more is intermediate risk; 8 or more is high risk
Surgical debridement within 6 hours is the mortality lever, not the antibiotic
AU empirical regimen: meropenem plus clindamycin plus vancomycin
explanation.pearls: The LRINEC score misses about a third of confirmed cases - if the clinical picture screams necrotising, do not let a low score reassure you.

sources.label: eTG complete: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections

stem:
A 46-year-old man with a family history of connective tissue disease presents with sudden tearing chest pain radiating between the shoulder blades. He is normotensive but pale and diaphoretic. CT aortogram shows an intimal flap involving the ascending aorta extending into the descending aorta with a small pericardial effusion measuring 8 mm.

On examination his right radial pulse is diminished compared to the left and there is a diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. He has no focal neurology and no leg ischaemia. Bedside echocardiogram shows no tamponade physiology but confirms the pericardial fluid.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108, BP 118/68 (right arm) 138/80 (left arm), RR 22, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temp 36.9 C
data_table.Investigations: Troponin 12 ng/L (<14); creatinine 88 micromol/L (60-110); Hb 132 g/L (130-170); D-dimer 6800 ng/mL
data_table.Imaging: CT aortogram: intimal flap from just above aortic root into descending aorta; 8 mm pericardial effusion; no rupture; visible root involvement
data_table.Echo: Aortic regurgitation moderate; pericardial fluid 8 mm without tamponade

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Immediate cardiothoracic surgical repair of the ascending aorta with cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Involvement of the ascending aorta (Stanford type A) is a surgical emergency because of risk of proximal extension into pericardium (tamponade), coronary arteries (MI) and aortic regurgitation. Perioperative medical management still requires impulse control - HR under 60 and SBP 100 to 120 mmHg via beta blockade first. Delaying for medical management alone is not sufficient for type A. (Source: eTG complete: Aortic dissection)

options.text: Medical management with IV labetalol and IV nitroprusside targeting SBP 100 to 120 mmHg
options.rationale: Medical management alone is the strategy for uncomplicated type B (descending), not for type A (ascending). Type A has 1 percent per hour mortality without surgery. Delaying repair for medical control alone would be fatal. (Source: eTG complete: Aortic dissection)

options.text: Thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) as first-line with cardiac monitoring in place
options.rationale: TEVAR is used for descending aortic dissection (type B) with complications. It cannot address the ascending aorta or the root without special hybrid procedures; open surgical repair is the standard for type A. (Source: eTG complete: Aortic dissection)

options.text: Emergency pericardiocentesis and admit to CCU on IV nitrate infusion with cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: There is no tamponade physiology so pericardiocentesis is not indicated; pericardiocentesis in a dissecting aorta can worsen bleeding into the pericardium by relieving tamponade tamponade. Nitrate infusion without beta blockade would worsen dP/dt. (Source: eTG complete: Aortic dissection)

options.text: Aspirin 300 mg plus ticagrelor 180 mg for presumed acute coronary syndrome
options.rationale: Antiplatelet loading is contraindicated in aortic dissection - it increases bleeding risk into the false lumen and pericardium. Troponin is not elevated and imaging shows a dissection, not ACS. (Source: eTG complete: Aortic dissection)

explanation.summary: Type A aortic dissection involves the ascending aorta and is a surgical emergency because of proximal extension into pericardium, coronaries and aortic valve. Untreated mortality is 1 percent per hour; open surgical repair is life-saving. Perioperative medical management still targets HR under 60 and SBP 100 to 120 mmHg via beta blockade first. Type B (descending only) is managed medically unless complicated.
key_points: Stanford type A: involves ascending aorta - open surgical repair
Stanford type B: descending only - medical impulse control, TEVAR if complicated
Medical impulse control still applies pre-op for both: HR under 60, SBP 100 to 120
Antiplatelets and pericardiocentesis are contraindicated in a dissecting aorta
explanation.pearls: Even in type A the pre-theatre plan is beta blockade first - vasodilator alone would raise dP/dt and worsen the tear before the surgeon arrives.

stem:
A 74-year-old woman is admitted from a nursing home with 24 hours of confusion, fever and reduced urine output. She has a chronic indwelling urinary catheter for outlet obstruction. She is on metformin for diabetes and no other regular medications.

On examination she is drowsy, has warm peripheries with a wide pulse pressure, and mottling of her thighs. Her catheter bag has cloudy foul-smelling urine. Chest is clear and abdomen is soft with suprapubic tenderness. She weighs approximately 60 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118 sinus tachycardia, BP 88/38, RR 26, SpO2 96 percent on 2 L nasal prongs, temp 39.4 C
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.6 x10^9/L (4-11); CRP 320 mg/L (<5); creatinine 218 micromol/L (baseline 78; 60-110); urea 18 mmol/L (2.5-7.5); lactate 4.6 mmol/L (<2); glucose 12.4 mmol/L; VBG pH 7.28; procalcitonin pending
data_table.Catheter urine: Cloudy foul-smelling; leucocyte esterase positive; nitrite positive; microscopy pending

lead_in: What is the correct sequence of actions in the first hour?

options.text: IV normal saline 30 mL per kg over 3 hours, wait for cultures before antibiotics
options.rationale: Antibiotic delay in septic shock is associated with increased mortality (up to 7 percent per hour). Cultures should not gate antibiotic timing - obtain cultures but give antibiotics within an hour of recognition. (Source: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock)
source_refs: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock

options.text: Blood cultures, arterial or venous lactate, then IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g
options.rationale: The Surviving Sepsis one-hour bundle applied in AU practice: obtain cultures before antibiotics (do not delay antibiotics more than 45 min), broad-spectrum antibiotics targeted to source (piperacillin-tazobactam plus gentamicin for urinary sepsis with sepsis physiology per eTG), 30 mL per kg crystalloid, lactate measurement, and noradrenaline if MAP under 65 after fluid resuscitation. Source control via catheter change is part of care. (Source: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock)
source_refs: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock

options.text: Empirical IV ceftriaxone 1 g plus oral metronidazole and 500 mL saline bolus, review in 6 hours
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone plus metronidazole under-covers Pseudomonas and enterococci in a catheter-associated urinary sepsis from a nursing home; oral metronidazole in a hypotensive patient is unpredictable in absorption. Fluid volume of 500 mL is insufficient; 30 mL per kg (about 1.8 L for 60 kg) is the initial target. (Source: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock)
source_refs: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock

options.text: Vasopressor infusion first via peripheral IV, then antibiotics, then cultures
options.rationale: Vasopressor before adequate fluid resuscitation is generally inappropriate; noradrenaline is added when MAP remains under 65 after fluid resuscitation. Skipping cultures forfeits pathogen data used to narrow therapy. (Source: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock)
source_refs: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock

options.text: Broad-spectrum antibiotics alone (piperacillin-tazobactam) without cultures, IV fluids or vasopressor
options.rationale: Antibiotic monotherapy without fluid resuscitation and cultures loses the physiological rescue components of the bundle. The AU one-hour bundle demands cultures, lactate, fluids, antibiotics, and vasopressor as a coordinated set. (Source: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock)
source_refs: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock

explanation.summary: AU sepsis management uses the one-hour bundle: obtain cultures without delaying antibiotics past 45 min, give broad-spectrum antibiotics matched to source, measure lactate, start 30 mL per kg crystalloid, and add noradrenaline if MAP under 65 after fluid. For catheter-associated urinary sepsis with shock, eTG recommends piperacillin-tazobactam plus gentamicin (single-dose aminoglycoside to cover Pseudomonas and gram-negatives). Source control includes catheter change.
key_points: One-hour bundle: cultures, lactate, antibiotics, fluid 30 mL per kg, vasopressor if MAP under 65 after fluid
Do not delay antibiotics for cultures past 45 min - each hour of delay increases mortality
Catheter-associated urosepsis with shock: piperacillin-tazobactam plus single-dose gentamicin
Source control (catheter change) is part of care, not optional
explanation.pearls: Antibiotic timing dominates mortality in septic shock - the target is under 45 minutes for the first dose.

sources.label: eTG complete: Sepsis and septic shock

stem:
A 68-year-old woman who presented 6 days ago with an anterior STEMI treated with primary PCI is on the coronary care unit. She has been mobilising well since day 3. At 4 am the nurse calls you because she suddenly becomes short of breath and hypotensive.

On arrival she looks unwell, has muffled heart sounds and is peripherally shut down. Jugular venous pressure is grossly elevated with y-descent absent. Bedside echocardiogram shows a large pericardial effusion with right ventricular diastolic collapse. There is no new ST-segment shift on ECG and CXR shows a modest widening of the cardiac silhouette compared with the film from 24 hours ago.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 68/40, RR 30, SpO2 92 percent on 15 L non-rebreather, temp 36.9 C
data_table.Investigations: Troponin 8200 ng/L (on downtrend from admission peak 45 000); Hb 96 g/L (was 118 yesterday); creatinine 108 micromol/L; INR 1.1; lactate 5.8 mmol/L; ECG anterior Q waves, no new ST shift
data_table.Medications: Aspirin 100 mg; ticagrelor 90 mg BD; atorvastatin 80 mg; ramipril 5 mg; bisoprolol 5 mg
data_table.Echo: Large pericardial effusion with RV diastolic collapse; regional wall motion abnormalities consistent with old anterior infarct; no ventricular septal defect visualised

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management?

options.text: Recurrent stent thrombosis - repeat coronary angiography and PCI and repeat as clinically indicated
options.rationale: Recurrent stent thrombosis presents with new ST elevation and rising troponin; her troponin is on downtrend and ECG shows no new ST shift. The tamponade physiology and falling Hb identify a mechanical complication rather than acute reinfarction. (Source: eTG complete: Post-MI mechanical complications)

options.text: Dressler syndrome - high dose aspirin and NSAIDs with colchicine, admit for observation and involve senior review
options.rationale: Dressler syndrome typically occurs 2 to 6 weeks post-MI with pleuritic chest pain, low-grade fever, small pericardial effusion without tamponade, and inflammatory markers up. This patient has tamponade physiology, falling Hb and is 6 days post-MI, which fits free wall rupture rather than post-cardiac injury pericarditis. (Source: eTG complete: Post-MI mechanical complications)

options.text: Post-MI ventricular septal defect - emergency surgery after intra-aortic balloon pump insertion
options.rationale: Post-MI VSD produces a new pan-systolic murmur with left-to-right shunt on echo colour flow, not a pericardial effusion with tamponade. Falling Hb into the pericardial space is not the VSD pattern. (Source: eTG complete: Post-MI mechanical complications)

options.text: Papillary muscle rupture - emergency mitral valve surgery and repeat as clinically indicated
options.rationale: Papillary muscle rupture causes acute severe mitral regurgitation with pulmonary oedema and a new murmur but not typically a large pericardial effusion. The echo pattern here is compressive pericardial effusion, not acute MR. (Source: eTG complete: Post-MI mechanical complications)

options.text: Left ventricular free wall rupture with cardiac tamponade - emergency cardiac surgery for pericardial evacuation
options.rationale: Sub-acute LV free wall rupture typically presents 3 to 7 days post-MI with tamponade physiology (JVP up, y-descent absent, hypotension, RV diastolic collapse on echo) and a falling haemoglobin without external bleeding. Definitive treatment is emergency surgical repair; pericardiocentesis can transiently relieve tamponade but reduces the compressive haemostasis and risks accelerated rebleeding. Antiplatelet load and dual antiplatelet therapy amplify the risk. (Source: eTG complete: Post-MI mechanical complications)

explanation.summary: Sub-acute LV free wall rupture is the leading post-MI mechanical complication at day 3 to 7 in a patient with a completed transmural infarct. It presents with sudden cardiovascular collapse and tamponade physiology (JVP elevation with absent y-descent, hypotension, RV diastolic collapse), often with a falling haemoglobin as blood accumulates in the pericardium. Definitive treatment is emergency surgical repair; pericardiocentesis is a bridge only, and DAPT amplifies bleeding risk.
key_points: Free wall rupture typically day 3 to 7 post-MI; peaks in transmural infarcts
Tamponade physiology plus falling Hb without external bleeding is the fingerprint
Emergency surgical repair is definitive; pericardiocentesis is temporising
Dressler syndrome is weeks later and rarely causes tamponade
explanation.pearls: A falling Hb into a growing pericardial effusion at day 6 post-MI is the free wall rupture story - pericardiocentesis alone lets the tamponade tamponade lose its haemostatic role.
